Why Citation Checking Matters

Every academic field depends on citations being honest pointers to evidence. When a citation points to a paper that does not actually say what is claimed, the error can propagate through later work that cites the citing paper rather than the original.

The problem with plausible citations

Language models are very good at producing citations that look right. The author names are real, the venue is real, and the title sounds like something those authors would write. But the specific claim attached to the citation may be absent from the paper, or present only in a weaker form.

Checking these by hand is tedious but necessary. A tool that fetches the cited paper and finds the most relevant passages makes the check faster without removing the human from the loop.

What a checker should do

A useful checker should show its evidence. It should quote the passage it relied on, link to where that passage appears in the source, and say clearly when it could not find support, rather than guessing.
